content_preview.title: Microsoft Expands Bug Bounty Program to Open Source and Third-Party Code, Pays Record $20 Million
content_preview.summary: Microsoft's bounty program paid over $20 million to 562 researchers this year after expanding scope to cover open-source software and third-party components.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

Microsoft has broadened its bug bounty program to cover vulnerabilities found in open-source software and third-party components, not just its own products, according to a [year-in-review post from the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC)](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/msrc/blog/2026/08/microsoft-bounty-program-year-in-review-more-than-20-million-awarded-biggest-year). The company said it paid out "more than $20 million awarded in our biggest year yet" to security researchers...

recommendations: Before merging, the human reviewer should write a corrections file at src/content/corrections/<YYYY-MM>/<article-slug>.json documenting the warning(s).
Consider adding trusted domains to config/source_allowlist.txt

editor_notes.content_quality: Well-structured 487-word News article using the standard Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know format. Clean, neutral, no editorializing. 'What We Don't Know' section appropriately flags that neither source names the specific open-source projects/components now in scope or details the triage process for third-party code.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 3 manifest entries had file != null (no failed fetches, no archive_fallback), and sha256 of each decompressed snapshot matched the manifest exactly (verified with `gunzip -c | sha256sum`) before reading. Read all three snapshots in full via gunzip + HTML text extraction, not WebFetch: (1) source-0.html.gz — microsoft.com/en-us/msrc/blog MSRC 'year in review' post (primary source). Confirms verbatim: '$20 million to 562 security researchers', 'Researchers from 64 countries', prior year '$17 million to 344 researchers from 59 countries', Zero Day Quest 'researchers from 20 countries ... Redmond campus ... nearly 700 vulnerability reports ... $2.3 million in awards', 'more than 300 additional reports and awarded more than $800,000'. Both blockquoted direct quotes in the article ('Security is a team sport...' and 'expanded our vulnerability awards portfolio...') appear verbatim in this snapshot — no paraphrase-as-quote issue. (2) source-1.html.gz — opensourceforu.com, published Aug 5 2026. Confirms 'programme year from July 1, 2025, to June 30, 2026' and '562 researchers received rewards, averaging approximately US$35,000 each' and the verbatim quoted phrase 'the growing reliance of modern products on open source software, external libraries, and interconnected cloud services, where vulnerabilities in upstream components can affect multiple Microsoft products'. (3) source-2.html.gz — itpro.com (Future plc), published Aug 5 2026, byline Emma Woollacott. Independently confirms the same Zero Day Quest reports/awards figures (nearly 700 reports, $2.3M) the article cites as 'confirmed by ITPro', and is the sole source for the per-vulnerability award caps ($100,000 cloud/Zero Day Quest, $250,000 endpoint/on-premises) which the article correctly attributes only to ITPro. No suspicious_patterns flagged in the manifest for any of the three sources (all null); no injection-like text found on manual read.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Every number, name, date, and quote in the article traces to a specific cited source and matches that source's text exactly — no hallucinated specifics, no misattribution between the three outlets, no orphan claims. The one automated finding (opensourceforu.com and itpro.com not present in config/source_allowlist.txt) is a curation gap, not a factual or attribution problem: itpro.com is a Future plc security/IT trade title (Future also publishes techradar.com, already allowlisted) with a named byline and standard editorial process; opensourceforu.com is an established (est. 2003, as Linux For You) open-source trade publication. Both outlets' reporting is fully corroborated by the primary MSRC source and by each other, so I am overriding the script's default APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS (which triggers automatically on any non-allowlisted domain, regardless of content quality) to APPROVE. This does not fit any APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS category (no misattributed/fabricated specific, no paraphrase-in-quotes, no wrong-outlet citation, no unsourced subordinate claim) — filing a corrections record here would be documenting a config gap, not informing readers of an actual error.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral throughout; attributes every claim inline ('according to MSRC', 'according to ITPro') rather than stating contested figures as fact.
editor_notes.originality: Searched src/content/articles/ for prior Microsoft bug-bounty coverage; none found. The only topically adjacent piece is 2026-07/23-github-cuts-public-bug-bounty-payouts-by-half..., which covers a different company and the opposite trend (GitHub cutting payouts vs. Microsoft raising them) — not a duplicate or overlapping angle.
concerns: opensourceforu.com and itpro.com are not yet in config/source_allowlist.txt; recommend adding both given they are established, reputable outlets (see factual_accuracy note) so future submissions citing them don't need a manual override.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Clean, well-sourced News piece. All three sources read in full and cross-verified; every figure and quote checks out verbatim. APPROVE.
